Does the police response depend on the topic of the protests, for example land rights versus political?

No, I don’t think so, there is freedom to protest, it’s ok for now. But if you specifically criticise the prime minister then the situation gets worse, which we saw during AL as well; you could criticise the AL but not PM Sheikh Hasina, they made her a god-like creature. A few people have spoken out against Tarique Rahman, they have been arrested, but this is not the general scenario. We hope that this government will allow freedom of speech because the government knows what happens if freedom of speech is actually attacked.

Can BNP members now operate freely? Does it differ at local or national level?

The situation is ok, I think. There are very few incidents but not like before.

Is there any more information you are able to give in relation to the political situation now?

If I could say one thing, the whole political situation is better than during the interim government and during the AL era. However, this was not the expectation after the July [2024] uprising. There were millions on the street in July [2024] and so many lives lost in order to build a new country. The situation is not that promising yet, we are not sure that the government is intending to bring that positive change. It is better than the AL and BNP is a better party, but they are unsure of the reform needed which is what the people wanted. As I mentioned, it is better, so we can still hope, even as the opposition we still have hope.

Interview with a Political Analyst at International NGO

Date: 8 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Political Analyst at International NGO; 3 CPIT officials

Can you give some background on your role within the organisation and current priorities?

I have been with [NGO] since 2012, the team works directly with the political parties, not with other organisations. The project started in 2011, and between then and 2024 only the AL has been in power. Now we are working in a situation where the AL it totally out of the political space.

Our objectives have been to support political parties to be more democratic, have a more inclusive organisation, promoting women [and] youth participation and also to help parties to have more horizontal and vertical dialogue, to have more communication across different tiers of their organisation. We help parties to build their own training units at district level. We help them build tools for conflict mitigation at district level. Around the election we helped them to build teams for campaign management, poll watcher management, and candidate training. The aim was to provide support to all but there was a different approach in relation to the party in power and others, according to party priorities. We worked with Jamaat e Islami [JeI] until 2013 but then JeI was pushed out of the political space until 2024, now we have again started working with them.

Since after the 2024 uprising, we have been working with the new political parties such as NCP [National Citizen Party], GOP [Gono Odhikar Parishad] and loosely with some left-wing political parties and continued work with BNP. However, until July 2024 our core work was with the AL and the opposition BNP, with some engagement with Jatiyo Party. Work with Jatiyo Party is currently on hold.

[Part of our work is] promoting political cooperation and tolerance. We have multiparty forums engaging all major political parties and they work together as a team. There have been wonderful activities and examples of working together (cooperation across parties) in 22 districts. We have many examples of co-operation, for example when police were harassing BNP members previously or if they were arrested, AL counterparts helped them to get bail or protect their properties from vengeance.

The same happened in August 2024 when the mobs were torching AL properties, BNP’s local leaders were protecting them and their properties, and this was due to their connections in multi-party forums. Multi-party forums work together to solve community problems (ie water, health, drainage). When they work together the problems get solved quicker.

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

Our program has changed.

What was your experience during the election period in relation to election-related violence?

There was no widespread political violence during the pre-election period. We promoted peaceful election processes across the parties. It was a realisation from opposition parties that if there was violence BNP, JeI etcetera would be the losers. We shared survey data with decision makers and campaign managers in political parties which found that 92% of people would not vote for a party engaged in violence. This enabled an understanding at grass roots levels.

We had a response system - if we suspected any violence was bubbling then we would contact the political parties to get them to internally resolve. We were afraid that the interim government (IG) was not really prepared to handle the situation if there was widespread violence. The IG control of police was weak, and police morale was low but because participating political parties did not want violence, it was one of the most peaceful election periods. Our interventions also helped to prevent political violence.

Has the newly elected BNP government implemented any recommendations from commissions formed under the interim government – if so, what?

Notes of interviews/meetings

The FFM team took notes of all meetings, which were then sent by email to the sources for review and approval. This email explained that if a source did not respond within a specific deadline, then CPIT would assume that the source was content with the notes as sent to them.

Of the 15 sources, 12 approved the notes with a number making amendments to the original drafts. 2 did not respond. One did not agree to publication of the notes.

One source provided footnotes when making amendments to the original drafts.

All sources are described and referred to according to their preference.

Terms of reference

A ‘Terms of Reference’ (ToR) is an outline of what the FFM seeks to cover. Prior to the FFM, the following topics were identified as relevant areas to explore. Note: the FFM focussed on the country situation since July 2024.

FFM introductory note

Aim of the fact-finding mission

The purpose of our visit is to obtain accurate and up-to-date information on the political situation since June/July 2024. We would like to meet with you to fill gaps in our knowledge on this subject.

The fact-finding mission team will be made up of 3 officials from the Country Policy and Information Team (CPIT).

About CPIT

CPIT is part of the UK Home Office, the government department responsible for immigration and asylum. We collect country information through both desk-based research and in-country visits.

The reports CPIT produce are published online. They are used primarily to assist UK immigration officials and judges involved in the asylum and human rights decision-making process.

More information about the CPIT’s range of products, including reports of other Fact-Finding Missions, can be found on our website: Country policy and information notes - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk).

Format of the fact-finding mission

During our visit we will be meeting a range of sources who can provide an informed view on the issues of interest, which are listed below.

We intend to take notes of the meetings. These notes may be made publicly available on the GOV.UK website and/or used in litigation proceedings.

However, we will not publish any information you provide if you do not consent. If you prefer that the information is not made publicly available, this will be respected.

We will provide you with an opportunity to review/amend the meeting notes to ensure they are an accurate reflection of our discussions. We will also ask you how you wish to be cited in our final report. If you are not willing to be named individually, you can choose to be identified in more general terms. Examples include: by the name of your organisation or department (‘an official from the Department of Health’), or by your occupation (an ‘academic’ or ‘journalist’).

Areas of interest

Government’s mandate, implementation of commission recommendations and new policies

Treatment of political groups since June/July /August 2024

Political violence

Arrest/detention/release of political prisoners

Law and order

I’ll pass you a copy of report we have done on reform.

What is the role of the auxiliary organisations (particularly student wings) in political parties and what are their activities?

Student wings had elections at all universities. They seem to have been fair. People were quite worried that the Jel student wing came out strongly but maybe that is to be expected as they have been very good at organising. The BNP and AL wings were more about patronage and violence and not really working for the welfare of students. If you focus on student housing, scholarships, and student nutrition then the student wing is more likely to get votes. It is interesting to see how student leaders develop and enter the mainstream.

Our research on student politics found it was a training ground for political parties. It really teaches them how to organise, how to do public speaking, reach out and build relations with mainstream parties. There are a number of people in mainstream parties who came through student politics. There have been debates on whether student politics should be banned or encouraged. We need to have a democratic and safe culture of student politics. There needs to a more constructive culture with democratic norms, and less violence and asking for money and all of that. That’s a different debate on how you ensure that there is a healthy student politics – we have to figure that out.

Was there any violence during student wing elections?

There was not that much compared to before; it was very peaceful. There were minor incidents before they released the results. On the whole, it was very peaceful which shows it can be done.

What were the levels of pre-election/election period intra- and inter-party violence? How does this compare to levels under the AL?

What has been coming out from our interviews is that the official reporting of violence is much less than what took place. The election complaints mechanism didn’t work very well. You will see in the EU report, they did a survey which found that people didn’t know they had a complaint office in their location, didn’t know about them at all or they didn’t know they could complain.

In interviews, people said that when they did lodge a complaint they weren’t taken seriously or that they took the complaint and nothing happened.

In Dhaka, this was reported in national media, a Jel candidate made a violent statement against women. There was a complaint filed that the speech was promoting violence against women. It went to the Chief Election Commissioner and nothing happened. This was a public incident of violence, we thought that because it was done publicly there would be some impact but there was no action from the election commission.

There was an incident where a rape by [a] BNP [member] was reported in Hatia due to the woman voting for the NCP. In the end, there was no evidence found to support this claim.

Compared to other elections, it has been more peaceful, and I haven’t heard of many incidents of violence against minorities.

Some Jel candidates put a religious angle on the election. For example, saying if you want to go to heaven you have to vote for us. The central leadership denied this and we don’t know if they gave any instruction to do this, but it happened more in rural areas.

There were also allegations of vote buying. All parties, except for left wing parties, spent a lot of money on votes.

In the election, so few women were nominated. The left wing parties did the best compared to other parties, about one third or half of their candidates were women.

What was the police response during the elections?

When people complained, the police didn’t take it seriously. Even BNP candidates complained that there was police bias towards Jel, and independent candidates complained there was a bias toward larger parties. So, there was a lot of jockeying before [the] election. The interim government said local administrations at all levels, including district commissioners, would be neutral. There was some reshuffling and each party accused the other of putting in their people and that the local administrations were biased.

Another thing during the IG, they took all locally elected people out and administrative people were appointed by officials.

There is a problem with the whole politicisation of the local administration. Each new government when it comes in will recruit people who are party loyalists. They will have background checks, looking at family connections, etc. This also happened during the AL period, and Jel were discriminated against.

Recently, there was a huge purge in the police of those perceived to be affiliated with the AL. There was a new batch of police officers supposed to be sworn in after one year of training, and the whole ceremony was cancelled the day before.

Also, each party tries to win favour by protecting minorities, they want to buy loyalty. We will have to see what the BNP does.

[This information was added after the meeting The AL claimed that they would protect the Hindu minority. This resulted in many of the Hindu voters supporting them.]

What is the police response to protest? Are there differences to their response under the AL, the IG and now?

During the IG, we seemed to have protests all the time for anything. It was quite disruptive, every day there was some sort of protest. I think people felt it was safer to protest. During the AL period, you had to get permission for demonstrations or protests, so there were no direct political protests as they would have had trouble. It was ok for environmental or women’s rights protests, they were allowed. There were also LGBTQI protests under the AL.

During the IG, there were some parties supporting the IG. Some movements were very conservative and targeted any protests they thought came from the LGBTQI community.
